title: Minor can consent confidentially to STI testing and treatment
vignette: A 17-year-old girl comes to the office for evaluation of worsening vaginal irritation and discharge. She has had multiple sexual partners in the past few months. The patient is adherent with oral contraceptives and inconsistently uses condoms. She has no prior medical conditions and takes no other medications. Urine pregnancy test is negative and urine gonorrhea test is positive. The patient does not want her parents to find out she is having sex and asks if the physician will tell her parents about today's visit. Which of the following is the most appropriate response to this patient?

clues.note: She is a minor (<18), who normally needs parental consent - EXCEPT for specific sensitive services such as STI care, for which minors can consent on their own in all states.
Gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted infection; testing and treatment of STIs is a recognized exception allowing minors to consent confidentially.

clues.text: does not want her parents to find out
clues.note: Confidentiality encourages adolescents to seek STI care; the physician should reassure her and directly answer her question rather than deflect.

clues.text: asks if the physician will tell her parents
clues.note: The correct response affirms confidentiality: she can consent to STI testing/treatment herself, so the physician will not notify her parents.

whatMatters: Minors can CONSENT to diagnosis and treatment of SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS on their own, confidentially, in all states. The physician should reassure the 17-year-old that her parents will not be notified because she can consent to STI care herself. Answer D.
strategy: Recognize the confidential-care exception: STIs (also usually pregnancy care, contraception, substance-use and mental-health treatment) let minors consent without parental involvement. The correct answer both preserves confidentiality AND directly answers her question. Reject options that threaten to notify parents (A, E), that wrongly require parental consent for treatment (B), or that deflect without answering/undermine confidentiality (C).

options.text: "Because gonorrhea is a reportable illness, I am obligated to report it to the health authorities and to your parents."
"I don't need to inform your parents that you are sexually active, but I will need their consent to prescribe antibiotic treatment."
"I recommend that you tell your parents about today's visit in case your symptoms become more serious."
"I will not notify your parents because you can consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections on your own."
"You can consent to treatment of gonorrhea, but because you are a minor, I am obligated to notify your parents."

eliminations.label: Report to authorities AND parents - false
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: claiming reportability obligates notifying parents. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: while some STIs are reportable to PUBLIC HEALTH authorities, that does not require or permit notifying parents; parental notification for STIs is not mandated. ✅ Correct if: explaining anonymous public-health reporting (not to parents).

eliminations.label: Need parental consent to treat - false
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: saying antibiotic treatment requires parental consent. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: minors can consent to STI TREATMENT themselves; parental consent is not required. ✅ Correct if: a non-exception treatment truly requiring parental consent.

eliminations.label: Recommend telling parents - deflects/undermines
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: urging her to disclose to parents. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it fails to answer her confidentiality question and pressures disclosure that isn't required; it can deter care-seeking. ✅ Correct if: shared decision-making when the patient asks for guidance on involving family (not an obligation).

eliminations.label: Obligated to notify parents - false
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: consent allowed but parents notified anyway. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: minors' confidential consent for STI care means parents are NOT notified; this contradicts the exception. ✅ Correct if: a situation with mandatory parental notification (not STIs).

reasoning: A 17-year-old normally needs parental consent, but STI care is a confidential exception
Gonorrhea (an STI) can be tested and treated with the minor's own consent
Confidentiality should be preserved and her question answered directly
-> reassure her that parents will not be notified; answer D
mechanism: Minors (age <18) generally require PARENTAL CONSENT for medical care, but consent is NOT required for a defined set of sensitive services because mandating parental involvement would deter adolescents from seeking needed care. These exceptions include DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT OF SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS (in all states), and - in most states - contraception, pregnancy care, and substance-use/mental-health treatment (emancipated minors and emergencies are separate exceptions). This patient has gonorrhea, an STI, so she can consent to testing and treatment CONFIDENTIALLY; the physician should reassure her that her parents will not be notified while directly answering her question. Although some STIs are reported anonymously to PUBLIC HEALTH departments for surveillance/partner tracing, this never entails notifying parents. Responses that require parental consent for treatment, threaten parental notification, or merely deflect are incorrect.
